body.heading: Same sound, different word
paragraphs: English is full of tricksters: words that sound exactly alike but are spelled differently and mean completely different things. They are called homophones. Your ears cannot tell them apart — only the meaning of the sentence can.
The most famous tricksters of all are there, their and they're. Master those three and the rest feel easy.

body.heading: The famous trio: there, their, they're
paragraphs: There — a place. The park is over there. (Tip: there hides the word here — both are places.)
Their — belonging to them. Their dog is friendly. (Tip: their hides the word heir — someone who inherits, who owns.)
They're — a short way of writing they are. They're coming to lunch. (Tip: if you can swap in 'they are' and the sentence still works, they're is your word.)

body.heading: More sound-alike pairs
paragraphs: See / sea — I can see the boat. The sea is calm today.
Here / hear — Come here, please. I can hear the birds.
Where / wear — Where is my hat? I wear it outside.
Buy / bye — We buy bread on Fridays. Wave and say bye.
Sun / son — The sun is warm. Her son is seven.
Right / write — Your answer is right. Please write your name.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Write one sentence using 'their' and one using 'they're'. Read them to a partner — can they tell which is which from the sound alone?
2. Which pair do you mix up most often? Make up a silly memory trick for it, like the ones in the trio section.

takeaway: Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning — and for there/their/they're, the swap test ('they are') and the hidden words (here, heir) settle every argument.

supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
